bib.title: 7. Enabling Agents to Take Action | Generative AI Design Patterns

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Generative AI Design Patterns, ch. 7 "Enabling Agents to Take Action" (P21 Tool Calling, P22 Code Execution, P23 Multiagent Collaboration), Valliappa Lakshmanan and Hannes Hapke, O'Reilly, 2025 (book). Time-of-writing statements are May/June 2025.
COVERAGE: 74217 of 74217 chars read (all extracted text, including the code blocks, Table 7-1 and footnotes). One tall page. Nothing skipped. Several code lines are truncated by the extraction at the right edge (for example "Ec", "Book me an economy class ticket from Mauritiu"). The figure images were not viewed; only their captions were read.

CLAIMS (ranked)

P21 Tool Calling
- The model never executes the tool. It emits a tool name and arguments, and client code invokes the function and returns the result.
  number: none
  setup: OpenAI Responses API walkthrough, 5 steps (implement function, pass tool definitions, client-side invocation, append result and call again, final response).
  quote: "For security reasons, the model doesn't actually call the tool. Instead, it emits tokens about which tool to call. You are expected to invoke the appropriate tool and provide the result back to the model."
  where: offset about 5k
- Tool count limit: accuracy falls as tools and parameters grow.
  number: 3 to 10 tools
  setup: stated as of June 2025, varies by LLM. This is the authors' observation and no data is given.
  quote: "The fewer functions and parameters you use, the more accurate the model will be—at the time of writing (June 2025), the limit seems to be 3 to 10 tools, depending on the LLM."
  where: Considerations, Improving reliability
- Reliability rules:
  - Use clear names and parameter descriptions.
  - Describe the policy for when to use each tool in the system prompt, for example search versus book, and how long search results stay valid.
  - Include examples of valid inputs.
  - Use enums so the Grammar pattern applies.
  - Don't make the model fill in what you know deterministically.
  - Return descriptive error messages so Reflection (P18) can retry.
  number: none
  quote: "Don't make the model fill in information that you know deterministically: if you already know a passenger's details, you could offload the burden of maintaining that from the model."
- Tool Calling plus Reflection mark the agentic threshold.
  number: none
  quote: "Tool Calling and Reflection are usually considered the threshold behaviors beyond which a GenAI application becomes an agentic application."
- ReAct is "just" CoT plus Tool Calling, so the book does not make it a separate pattern.
  number: none
  quote: "Because ReAct is "just" a combination of CoT and Tool Calling, we didn't make it a separate pattern in this book."
- Tool Calling is an extension of Pattern 2 (Grammar). Models are trained to emit a special token for a call. The book's illustrative format is `[CALL_TOOL: book_flight, TK 161, 2025-06-12, Economy]`. A footnote says real formats are JSON.
- Use cases listed:
  - up-to-date knowledge (RAG covers static, pre-indexable knowledge only)
  - personalization
  - enterprise APIs
  - calculations (calculators, GIS, solvers)
  - ReAct
- Provider schemas differ. Anthropic uses `input_schema`. OpenAI uses `parameters`. Llama nests under `function` with `parameters`, and shows `"strict": true`. Advice: use an LLM-agnostic framework (PydanticAI, LangChain, LangGraph, LiteLLM) and avoid the provider client API unless you have no other choice.
- Naming: Toolformer (the inventors), Tool Use (Ng, Anthropic), Function Calling (OpenAI, Gemini). The authors prefer "tool" because it also covers APIs and remote proxies, and "calling" because the client does the invoking.
- MCP split: MCP simplifies Steps 1-2 (supplying tool details). A client framework such as LangGraph simplifies Steps 3-4. Step 5 is unchanged. A tool is defined by `@mcp.tool` with a self-descriptive name, parameters and docstring. Transports: stdio for Python-only clients, streamable-http for other languages or machines. The server can be deployed on Cloud Run, Fargate or Azure Container Instances.
- MCP limits (May 2025), all three flagged as likely to date:
  - Security: no authentication or authorization enforcement. "MCP... is more of a language interoperability protocol—it doesn't enforce any security principles." Cloudflare extended its Workers OAuth Provider Library to fill the gap.
  - Collaboration: communication is mostly one way. Google A2A and IBM ACP (April/May 2025) add agent-to-agent communication.
  - Streaming: tool calls can be long. number: 30-60 seconds. quote: "Standard MCP calls, at the time of writing, are terminated in 30–60 seconds, depending on network configurations." The streamable HTTP transport enables streaming.
- Prompt injection grows with tool use. "The attack area increases with the number of round trips between the LLM and the tools they invoke." Six guardrail patterns from Beurer-Kellner et al. 2025:
  - Action-Selector: a predefined action set, with no feedback from actions to the agent.
  - Plan-Then-Execute: a fixed plan, and tool feedback cannot change it.
  - Map-Reduce: isolated subagents handle each piece of untrusted input. The reduce step uses no LLM or a constrained selector.
  - Dual-LLM: a privileged planner with tools, plus a sandboxed LLM with no tools for untrusted data.
  - Code-Then-Execute: the agent writes a program with fixed control flow, which can spawn unprivileged LLMs.
  - Context-Minimization: remove unnecessary content, including the original user prompt in later steps.
  quote: "trying to guard LLMs with Tool Calling against prompt injection is an ongoing challenge."
- Tool Calling fits tasks "invoked by sending a few parameters to a function". If the input is a DSL such as SQL, use P22.
- Worked example: a weather agent (Chicago rain question) with two MCP tools, NWS `get_weather_from_nws` (lat/lon to grid point to forecast) and `latlon_geocoder` (Google Maps). It uses `create_react_agent` with claude-3-7-sonnet-latest, and a few-shot ReAct-style system prompt.
- Named MCP servers: GitHub, Sentry, Zapier AI Actions.

P22 Code Execution
- Use it when the target system is driven by a DSL or a long phrase, not a few parameters. The LLM generates the DSL and a postprocessor (typically in a sandbox) executes it. It can also run as ReAct steps.
  quote: "Tool Calling is insufficient when the function to be called takes a long phrase in a DSL as input instead of a short list of parameters."
- Models are good at Matplotlib, SQL and Mermaid, and poor at drawing graphs or annotating images directly.
- Database updates: "it's easier to have the LLM generate the SQL and send it to your database as a single transaction, rather than expecting the LLM to be able to maintain data integrity."
- Worked example: NCAA 2025 tournament results go to Graphviz DOT via a one-shot prompt. The prompt names subgraphs `cluster_xxx`. The DOT file is rendered with `dot -Grankdir=LR -Tpng tournament.dot -o tournament.png`. Results come from web search (tool calling) or Basic RAG (P6).
- Sandbox advice:
  - Isolated environment with constraints on CPU, memory, network access and execution time.
  - Monitor for infinite loops and resource exhaustion.
  - Implement with Docker, VMs or specialized runtimes.
  - Validate before executing (syntax check, static analysis, formal correctness checking).
  - Keep sandbox containers up to date, because "vulnerabilities in the sandbox OS or the sandbox isolation mechanisms could allow access to host systems."
  - Risks remain: resource exhaustion, data exfiltration, harmful-code prompts.
- Feed compiler and runtime errors back to the LLM (Reflection, P18).
- Reliability caveat. quote: "At the time of writing (June 2025), code execution environments tend to be unreliable unless they have very tightly controlled inputs or they run in a sandbox that allows for Reflection. Code Execution works better when the generated code is a narrow DSL and the execution environment involves a parser."
- Examples named: Claude uses Mermaid as an intermediate format. Gemini generates Pandas for financial analysis.

P23 Multiagent Collaboration
- Single-agent limits named:
  - cognitive bottlenecks (finite context)
  - decreasing parameter efficiency
  - limited reasoning depth. quote: "You'll be more successful if you can treat reasoning as breadth-first search and allow it correspondingly more tokens."
  - domain adaptation (fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting)
- Benefits claimed: task decomposition, parallel processing, hierarchical problem-solving, domain expertise, functional specialization. Horizontal scaling, replaceable agents, redundancy, cross-verification, and "emergent capabilities". The emergent-capability and mutual-learning claims are asserted without data.
- Three architectures plus hybrid:
  - Hierarchical: executive-worker or multilevel. Needs task decomposition, priority scheduling and output aggregation. Simplest form is prompt chaining or a sequential workflow, "a hierarchy where there is only one leaf node and all the other nodes have exactly one child." Example is a LangChain SequentialChain (paragraph, title, keywords).
  - Peer-to-peer: consensus or voting, with distributed consensus, peer discovery and reputation systems. Example is a CrewAI task, up to 3 rounds then majority vote, with senior, content and research editors.
  - Market-based: auctions and utility maximisation. Sealed-bid used-car example and an English auction with a minimum price and increments. Needs auction algorithms, utility functions or a virtual currency.
- Human-in-the-loop: make one agent a proxy for a human who resolves conflicts. P2P and market systems need conflict resolution.
- Use cases:
  - Parallel execution. quote: "This is, by far, the most common, useful, and least complex use of multiple agents."
  - Complex reasoning
  - Multistep problem solving
  - Collaborative content creation
  - Adversarial verification (red team and blue team)
  - Specialized-domain integration
  - Self-improving systems (evaluator agents)
- AG2 example (framework originated at Microsoft): a ninth-grade workbook pipeline in 8 steps. A human proxy sends a topic to a Task Assigner (a router: "a group of workers is fronted by a classifier"). It picks HISTORIAN or MATH WRITER at temperature 0 with a Pydantic `Literal` response_format (Grammar). The writer drafts. A 5-agent RoundRobin review panel (district_admin, school_admin, secretary, conservative_parent, liberal_parent) with `max_rounds=len(reviewers)+1` so each speaks once. The secretary summarises into directives, and the writer rewrites with `max_turns=2` (one round of clarifying questions). Model config shown: gemini-2.0-flash or gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.2.
- Considerations:
  - Anthropic recommends simple, composable patterns over complex frameworks.
  - Prefer peer agents in parallel. This cuts wall-clock time but "the overall computational overhead remains the same."
  - Communication cost: "The computational cost of coordination increases nonlinearly with the number of agents."
  - Consistency across agents is hard. Specialisation trades consistency complexity for communication complexity.
  - Feedback loops amplify errors and biases. Agents may optimise individual objectives over system goals.
  - Errors compound: "the longer the chain of steps, the less likely it is that you'll get a successful task completion."
  - Failure rate. number: 40% to 80%. setup: 2025 analysis of multiagent systems (Cemri et al. 2025), 14 failure modes in 3 categories. quote: "A 2025 analysis found that 40% to 80% of tasks in multiagent systems fail due to issues with system design, agent coordination, or quality control." No benchmark or model detail is given in the chapter.
  - The three categories are specification issues, interagent misalignment and task verification. Sub-modes: repeating steps, losing context, failing to recognise task completion, conversation resets, no clarification requests, task derailment, withholding information, ignoring other agents, reasoning-action mismatch, and premature termination.
  - Improving these areas is not enough, so fundamental changes are needed.
  - Recommendation. quote: "if you can employ UX design, introduce a human-in-the-loop, or set customer expectations so that a single-agent system suffices, then we recommend that you choose one of those approaches instead."
- A2A sidebar: agents from different frameworks and machines interoperate. Pydantic AI `agent.to_a2a()` served with uvicorn on port 8093. Called from a TypeScript Mastra agent via `@mastra/client-js` `A2A`, `sendTask` and `streamTaskUpdates`.
- Pattern taxonomy in References: Ng (May 2024) lists Reflection, Tool Use, Planning and Multiagent. OpenAI adds LLM-as-Judge, Parallelization, Router and Guardrails. Anthropic separates workflows (pre-specified, for example chaining and Router) from agents (autonomous orchestration). Google's 2025 whitepaper names CoT, ReAct and ToT as cognitive patterns. Devin is cited as a subagent orchestrator (plan, code, sandbox execute, debug, web search).

LIMITS: No quantitative evaluation of any pattern except the 40-80% failure figure, which is cited and not reproduced. The 3-10 tool limit is an unsupported observation. The authors concede that MCP's gaps may be fixed or MCP replaced ("MCP is rapidly evolving"). Dated by now (Nov 2026):
- the MCP limits, including the 30-60 s timeout
- A2A and ACP status
- the model names (gpt-4.1, claude-3-7-sonnet-latest, gemini-2.0-flash)
- the LangChain `LLMChain` and `SequentialChain` code, which is legacy
The chapter's code-execution reliability claim is stated for June 2025. The Cemri paper had an updated version while the book was in press (footnote 3).

BUILDS ON: Toolformer (Schick et al. 2023). ReAct (Yao et al. 2022). Beurer-Kellner et al. 2025 (six prompt-injection design patterns). Cemri et al. 2025 (multiagent failures). Wang et al. 2021 (CodeT5). Chen et al. 2021 (HumanEval). Hyunh and Lin 2025 (code-generation survey). Andrew Ng (May 2024 agentic patterns). Anthropic 2024 blog on composable patterns. Google 2025 multiagent whitepaper. MCP (Anthropic) and A2A (Google). Also AlphaCode, Codex and StarCoder.

CODE (verbatim, short; the extraction truncates long lines)
- Tool dispatch (OpenAI Responses):
  `tool_call = response.output[0]`
  `if tool_call.name == "book_flight":`
  `     args = json.loads(tool_call.arguments)`
- Returning the result:
  `input_messages.append(tool_call)  # append model's function cal`
  `input_messages.append({ "type": "function_call_output", "call_id": tool_call.call_id, "output": json.dumps(result) })`
- MCP tool and transports:
  `@mcp.tool()`
  `mcp.run(transport="stdio")`
  `mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")`
- MCP client plus ReAct agent:
  `agent = langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent("anthropic:claude-3-7-sonnet-latest", client.get_tools())`
  using `MultiServerMCPClient` from `langchain_mcp_adapters.client`
- DOT render:
  `dot -Grankdir=LR -Tpng tournament.dot -o tournament.png`
- Router with grammar:
  `class TaskAssignmentResponse(BaseModel): writer: Literal['HISTORIAN', 'MATH WRITER']`
  with `temperature=0.0, response_format=TaskAssignmentResponse`
- Round robin:
  `pattern = RoundRobinPattern(initial_agent=reviewers[0], agents=reviewers, user_agent=None, ...)`
  `initiate_group_chat(pattern=pattern, max_rounds=len(reviewers)+1, ...)`
- A2A:
  `app = agent.to_a2a()`
  `uvicorn agent_to_a2a:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8093`
- CrewAI consensus: the Task description reads "Engage in up to 3 rounds of discussion... If consensus is not reached after 3 rounds, a majority vote will determine the..."

FIGURES (captions come from figures.py; images not viewed)
- Fig 7-1 "How Tool Calling works". Good for the client-side invocation loop.
- Fig 7-2 "Difference between MCP client and servers". Good for the MCP topology.
- Fig 7-3 "In Code Execution, the LLM generates code that is executed in a sandbox environment to produce the final response". Good for P22.
- Fig 7-4 "Part of an image depicting the results of a basketball tournament" and Fig 7-5 "Depiction of the results of the four games in the Elite Eight". Example output only, low value.
- Fig 7-6 "Collaboration among agents in the end-to-end example of creating educational content". Good for the router, panel, secretary and rewrite flow (8 numbered steps).
- Table 7-1 (Patterns for enabling action) is a three-row summary of problem, solution and usage.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions in the PDF. The text extraction is clean but truncates long code lines. The tool_call example and the first code block (the `book_flight` call) lost their listings in the prose flow and appear only in the appended code dump. The numbers 30-60 s, 3-10 tools and 40-80% are single-source claims with no setup beyond what is quoted. The book's A2A and MCP statements are for May/June 2025.
